title: Power BI October 2026 Feature Summary
text: Last month, we shared a packed September update alongside the European Microsoft Fabric + SQL Community Conference. Even so, the Power BI team has continued delivering new capabilities, and we didn't want to wait another month to share them. This update includes enhancements across Copilot and AI, reporting, and semantic models, helping users create richer reports, streamline workflows, and get more value from their data. Table of Contents Copilot and AI Create Power BI reports with custom visuals using skills for Fabric (Generally Available) Reporting Gantt chart (Preview) List slicer with dropdown option (Preview) Chart plot area background color (Generally Available) Auto-expand hierarchy axis with field parameter support (Generally Available) Personal bookmarks keep column widths (Generally Available) Semantic models More accurate surge protection with semantic models That’s a wrap! Copilot and AI   Create Power BI reports with custom visuals using skills for Fabric (Generally Available) The Power BI Report Authoring skill now extends natural-language report authoring to custom visuals, helping teams create reports that meet specialized business and design requirements with less manual configuration. Ask the agent to add a visual, bind it to report data, apply formatting, and validate the visualization. The skill can use supported custom visuals already added to a report, including visuals imported from a file, and it can help identify an AppSource visual when the report needs a capability that core visuals don’t provide. This reduces time spent finding visual identifiers, editing report files, and troubleshooting field mappings, so report authors can focus on selecting the right presentation for the business question. Learn more in the  Power BI Report Au thoring skill overview  and  Install Skills for Fabric  guidance. Reporting Gantt chart (Preview) The Gantt visual is a new core visual for Power BI reports that lets you show tasks and progress on a time-based axis. Use it to plan projects, track schedules, or compare activities across categories directly in your report. Figure: Gantt visual showing a project schedule grouped by Planning, Development, Testing, and Deployment phases from January to April 2025, with the Format visual pane open to the Visual tab. The visual includes: Plotting of bars showing the duration of each row with progress formatting and milestones to mark key -dates. Axis with custom formatting and range controls, so you can set the start and end dates, adjust the date and time format, and choose the units that appear on the axis. Bar colors cascade naturally by category, which keeps related tasks visually grouped without extra configuration. You can add more columns next to the task list to show fields such as owner, status, or duration. A zoom axis lets report readers focus on a specific window of time and then return to the full range. To try the Gantt visual, enable it in Power BI Desktop under  File  >  Options and settings  >  Options  >  Preview features , and then restart Power BI Desktop. To learn more and try it in your reports, refer to the  Gantt vis ual  documentation. List slicer with dropdown option ( Preview ) The list slicer now includes a dropdown mode that makes long lists easier to navigate and active filters easier to review. Enable Show selected first to pin current selections to the top of the dropdown, eliminating the need to scroll through every item to confirm what is filtered. The button slicer also supports Show selected first , providing the same quick view of active selections in either slicer style. Figure: List slicer in dropdown mode showing selected values as dismissible pills and the Show selected first option. The dropdown carries over the formatting you've already applied to the list slicer items, and you can now customize the height and width of the dropdown drawer to fit your report layout. The search box also has more formatting options, so you can match the slicer to the look you want across background, border, and text styles. Each selection appears as a pill outside the dropdown that shows the item name and a dismiss button, so report readers can remove a value with one click. When selections exceed the available space, a count pill shows how many more values are selected, so you can see the total without opening the dropdown. When you use Select all and then clear one or more items, the slicer makes the resulting filter state explicit. Cleared values appear as Not (item) pills, showing that Power BI is excluding those values rather than including every remaining item individually. If you do not clear any items,  S elect all behaves like no selection and does not filter other visuals. To learn more, refer to the  Slicers in Power BI  documentation. Chart plot area background color (Generally A vailable) The plot area of bar, column, line, area, combo, ribbon, waterfall, and scatter charts now supports a single fill color and conditional formatting in addition to the existing background options. A solid color can improve visual separation, while conditional formatting can use a measure or field value to make changes in the data easier to recognize. Figure: Bar chart with the Plot area background formatting pane open, showing the new Background color and Transparency options. To learn more, refer to the Customize vis ualizatio ns in a Power BI report  documentation. Auto-expand hierarchy axis with field parameter support (Generally A vailable) Bar, column, and line charts now support auto-expand for the hierarchy axis when you add more than one column to the axis, and the hierarchy axis now works with field parameters. Figure: Column chart using a field parameter on the axis with Auto expand turned on in the X-axis formatting pane. This matches the existing auto-expand behavior in the slicer and matrix visuals, so hierarchy interactions stay consistent across your report. Add a field parameter to the axis so you can quickly switch between a single column and any combination of columns as the hierarchy, without rebuilding the visual. Report viewers can drill up, drill down, or move across hierarchy levels from a slicer, allowing them to explore the data based on the question they want to answer. The same behavior is available when viewers use Personalize this visual to change the chart’s axis fields. Figure: Selecting a field in the Category parameter slicer updates the column chart axis and the matrix hierarchy at the same time. The animation shows a report page with a Category parameter slicer, a column chart, and a matrix. When you select  Country in the slicer, the column chart updates to show Sales by Country with one bar per country, and the matrix updates to show the Country level of the hierarchy. Selecting Segment or Product instead swaps the chart axis and matrix hierarchy to that field. When you make multiple selections, the hierarchy expands automatically, so a single slicer controls the fields used across both visuals without requiring other changes to the report. To learn more, refer to the  Customize X-axis and Y-axis p roperties ,  D rill mode in the Power BI service  and  Create field parame ters  documentation. Personal bookmarks keep column widths (Generally A vailable) Personal bookmarks now preserve visual column widths, so you can return to the exact table or matrix layout you saved instead of resizing columns again. This includes reordered and resized columns, helping you maintain a consistent personal view each time you apply the bookmark. Figure: Save a personal bookmark to preserve your report’s table column widths. To learn more, refer to the Personal boo kmarks in Power BI  documentation. title: Fabric Policies: Granular governance at scale (Preview)
text: As Microsoft Fabric grows across teams, workspaces, and capacities, governance becomes harder to manage with broad tenant-wide switches alone because governance models are not one-size-fits-all. Fabric Policies provide granular controls that can fit your governance model by defining what actions are allowed, to whom and where . The result is governance that scales with your Fabric estate. Teams keep the flexibility they need to work; capacity admins can protect the resources they manage, and central administrators gain consistent controls and visibility across the organization. Fabric Policies help organizations: Match controls to organizational boundaries - Apply organization-wide rules at tenant scope and resource-specific rules at capacity scope. Protect sensitive actions without slowing routine work -  Keep approved self-service available while restricting higher-risk actions to the right users and context. Apply consistent guardrails at scale -  Manage policies centrally through Policy Sets, Policies Center, auditing, and public APIs. What you can govern Fabric Policies currently provide controls for item creation, external data sharing (coming soon), and selected security-sensitive workspace settings. Control item creation by capacity Capacity admins can set a policy for any Fabric item type in workspaces assigned to their capacity (Power BI item creation is not yet enforced). An admin can allow the Data Engineering security group to create Dataflow Gen2 items in selected data platform workspaces and the AI Builders security group to create Data agent items in selected AI workspaces. Matching requests proceed; requests that do not match a complete Allow rule are blocked. This control supports a gradual Fabric rollout. Organizations can make specific item types available to approved teams and workspaces as their governance requirements are met, rather than enabling every item type everywhere at once. Item creation requires both controls to allow the request: the applicable Fabric item creation setting and the active Item creation policy. Figure: Advanced Item creation policy with separate Allow rules for Dataflow Gen2 and Data agent. Protect security-sensitive workspace settings Fabric admins can protect selected settings without removing broader workspace administration capabilities. An admin can allow the Central IT team to edit Outbound access protection , Inbound access protection , and Apply customer-managed keys (CMK) in sensitive workspaces. Other workspace admins can continue to edit the rest of the settings. The policy refines what existing workspace admins can change; it does not grant the Workspace Admin role. Govern external data sharing (Coming Soon) Fabric admins can support partner collaboration while controlling who can share, which workspaces the data comes from, its sensitivity label, and the recipient email domain. An admin can allow the Finance security group to share items labeled Confidential from Finance workspaces with recipients at CALDOVA.com. Sharing proceeds only when all configured conditions match; other requests are blocked. External sharing can be allowed by either the existing External data sharing tenant setting or a matching and active policy rule. How Policies work On Policy Set creation, an administrative scope is selected, such as the tenant or a capacity. This defines the available policy types and the administrator role required to activate the Policy Set for that scope. Figure: Policy Set overview showing tenant or capacity scope. For each policy, administrators choose  Allow all , Block all , or Advanced . Advanced policies use an allow-based model: All conditions within a rule must match. A match on any complete rule allows the action. If no rule matches, the action is blocked. Once the Policy Set is activated, Fabric evaluates its policies whenever a governed action occurs within that scope. Only one Policy Set can be active for a tenant or an individual capacity. Activating a replacement changes which definitions govern that scope. Existing access requirements remain in effect. Policies do not grant Fabric roles, workspace access, or item permissions. A user must first have the access required for the action; the policy then adds a governance decision for that action and context. Fabric Policies are available in preview for supported Fabric capacities and workspaces. Standard Fabric capacity and workspace requirements apply. Get started with Fabric Policies In Admin portal > Tenant settings , enable Policies (Preview) . In a Fabric-capacity-backed workspace, create a Policy Set and choose Tenant or Capacity scope. Configure a policy with Allow all , Block all , or Advanced Allow rules, then review the users, actions, and workspaces covered. Activate the Policy Set as an administrator of the target scope. For capacity scope, select a capacity you administer. Review the related Fabric setting and policy together, then verify the active result in OneLake Catalog > Policies Center . For repeatable deployment across environments or capacities, use Fabric REST APIs to automate Policy Set and policy management at scale. API operations and activation remain subject to the required item permissions and administrator role. Policies best practices and management Design Advanced policies around every allowed scenario. List every user, item type, and workspace combination that must continue to work. Because Advanced policies are allow-based, a request is blocked when no complete rule matches. Align capacity policies with capacity ownership. Item creation policies govern workspaces assigned to the selected capacity. Each capacity can have its own active Policy Set, giving capacity admins control within their resource boundary. Review policy coverage whenever workspaces move between capacities. Use a dedicated management workspace. A Policy Set can be hosted in one supported Fabric-capacity-backed workspace and activated for a different capacity. A dedicated workspace can simplify access, ownership, and lifecycle management across multiple capacities. Separate editing from activation. People with Read , or the workspace Viewer role, can view a Policy Set. People with Read and Write , or a workspace Contributor , Member , or Admin role, can edit it. Activation still requires the administrator role for the target scope: Fabric admin for tenant scope or capacity admin for capacity scope. Validate before broad rollout. Start with representative users and workspaces and review each allowed scenario. Monitor and refine. Use Policies Center to review active policies and the Microsoft 365 Audit Log to follow Policy Set and rule lifecycle operations. Conclusion As Microsoft Fabric adoption scales across teams, workspaces, and capacities, governance must scale with it. Fabric Policies provide the flexibility to apply the right controls in the right contexts while maintaining a consistent governance model across the organization. By combining centralized oversight with granular policy enforcement, organizations can confidently expand their Fabric footprint without sacrificing security or control. Learn more about policies.

title: Databricks ADBC connector for Power BI and Microsoft Fabric (Generally Available)
text: This release is part of the broader ODBC-to-ADBC transition for Power Query connectors described in the Transition from ODBC to ADBC drivers in Power BI and Microsoft Fabric documentation. What’s new Existing connections in your semantic models, dataflows, and paginated reports continue to work unchanged — the migration path is currently opt-in per connection, per workspace, or per tenant. Highlights: Improved security - ADBC drivers incorporate security enhancements, such as memory safety and garbage collection. No changes to existing behavior - This transition moves away from the embedded ODBC drivers that ship with Power BI. It does not change behavior for the ODBC connector when you use a separately installed ODBC driver. Efficient large dataset support - ADBC provides a set of standard interfaces for interacting with Arrow data, which is especially efficient at fetching large datasets with minimal overhead and no serialization or copying. Supported authentication - Databricks ADBC supports OAuth (user), OAuth (M2M / Client Credentials), and Microsoft Entra ID. Connectors covered by this release Connector Previous driver New driver (GA) Databricks Simba Spark ODBC Databricks ADBC Azure Databricks Simba Spark ODBC Databricks ADBC How to try it You can test the ADBC driver now. We suggest you start soon to help ensure the eventual deprecation of ODBC and migration to ADBC runs smoothly. There are three ways to begin validating ADBC, ordered by how much control you want. 1. Opt in per connection using Implementation="2.0" The fastest way to compare ADBC and ODBC for a specific report or dataset. Add the Implementation="2.0" option to the source step in your Power Query expression: Source = Databricks.Catalogs("adb-1234567890.1.azuredatabricks.net", "/sql/1.0/warehouses/<warehouse-id>", [Implementation="2.0"]) Refresh the dataset and compare row counts, column types, and totals against your production baseline. If you want to force a side-by-side comparison against ODBC, use Implementation="1.0" . 2. Override the default for a validation workspace If you want to validate several reports together, a workspace admin can turn ADBC on for a single workspace while the rest of the tenant continues to use the legacy driver. Publish the reports you want to test into that workspace and run your normal refresh schedule. 3. Enable ADBC by default at the tenant level When you’re confident with the results, the tenant admin can enable Users can connect to data sources by using Apache Arrow database connectivity (ADBC) in the Admin portal. New connections across the tenant will use the ADBC driver by default, and Desktop and the service stay aligned on the same driver. What to expect during validation The ADBC driver is designed as a compatibility-preserving replacement for the Simba Spark ODBC driver. Validate your key reports in Desktop before enabling ADBC at the tenant level and report any regressions to adbcmigration@microsoft.com . Explore Transition from ODBC to ADBC drivers in Power BI and Microsoft Fabric for more information. What’s next The Power BI service will move from ODBC to ADBC through the first quarter of 2027. We recommend that you start validating today, so the tenant-level move is a non-event when it lands. We’d love your feedback Try the new Databricks ADBC driver. If anything looks different from what you'd expect — a refresh that fails, a total that changed, a performance regression — send the tenant ID, connector, M expression, and what you observed to adbcmigration@microsoft.com . Get started this week: Read the Databricks connector documentation . Install the latest Power BI Desktop. Pick one production report on Databricks and add Implementation="2.0" to its source step. Compare row counts, column data types, and key totals against your production baseline. Report anything unexpected to adbcmigration@microsoft.com .

title: File Data Ingestion with Materialized Lake Views in Microsoft Fabric (Preview)
text: File data ingestion with materialized lake views (MLVs) in Microsoft Fabric is now available in preview. Instead of building separate ingestion pipelines to move raw files into tables, you can now ingest CSV and Parquet files directly from OneLake into a materialized lake view and make your bronze layer part of the same declarative pipeline as the rest of your medallion architecture. This capability builds on the recent announcement of Materialized Lake Views in Microsoft Fabric (Generally Available) , extending the simplified approach from table-based transformations to raw file ingestion. Why this matters Until now, you had to build and maintain a separate ingestion layer before you could get the benefits of MLVs, which had to start from tables. To get raw files into that first table, you'd reach for a shortcut transformation, a data pipeline, or a notebook load which is a separate step to build and operate before your declarative pipeline could even begin. File data ingestion removes that step. Point a materialized lake view at a folder of files, and Fabric handles the ingestion, materializes the results as a Delta table, and plugs it straight into the same lineage, scheduling, data quality, and monitoring that power the rest of your medallion architecture. One programming model, from raw files to gold. If you've referred to Simplifying Medallion Implementation with Materialized Lake Views , there was a missing link in the first mile: bronze, expressed declaratively. Now we have resolved that. What is file data ingestion? A file-ingesting materialized lake view is defined with a USING OneLake_Files clause instead of an AS SELECT query. You describe the source folder and format, and Fabric materializes it: CREATE MATERIALIZED LAKE VIEW bronze.raw_orders USING OneLake_Files OPTIONS (  'format' = 'csv',  'path'   = 'abfss://SalesWorkspace@onelake.dfs.fabric.microsoft.com/SalesLake.Lakehouse/Files/orders/',  'header' = 'true' ) TBLPROPERTIES (  'schema_mode'  = 'DYNAMIC',  'refresh_mode' = 'APPEND_ONLY' ); That single statement gives you a queryable, refreshable bronze table. In preview, file data ingestion supports: CSV and Parquet source files. Recursive folder ingestion — files in nested subfolders are picked up automatically. Schema evolution with DYNAMIC mode, or a pinned schema with FIXED mode which gets auto detected during creation. Source traceability — every row carries a __filepath__ column recording that records its source file. CSV parsing supports the header and delimiter options; additional CSV options and further capabilities are on the roadmap. Build a complete medallion — From files to gold Because a file-ingesting view behaves like any other materialized lake view once created, you can layer transformations on top of it and let Fabric orchestrate the whole chain in dependency order: -- Bronze: ingest raw files directly from OneLake CREATE MATERIALIZED LAKE VIEW bronze.raw_orders USING OneLake_Files OPTIONS ('format' = 'csv', 'path' = 'abfss://…/Files/orders/', 'header' = 'true') TBLPROPERTIES ('schema_mode' = 'DYNAMIC', 'refresh_mode' = 'APPEND_ONLY'); -- Silver: clean and enforce data quality declaratively CREATE MATERIALIZED LAKE VIEW silver.orders ( CONSTRAINT valid_amount CHECK (amount > 0) ON MISMATCH DROP ) AS SELECT id, customer, CAST(amount AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS amount FROM bronze.raw_orders; -- Gold: aggregate for reporting CREATE MATERIALIZED LAKE VIEW gold.daily_sales AS SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS total FROM silver.orders GROUP BY customer; Fabric records the dependency from silver.orders → bronze.raw_orders → the source folder and refreshes them in order. When new files land, the change flows through silver to gold — no glue code, no orchestration to maintain. Trace every file through lineage File data ingestion is fully integrated into the materialized lake views lineage experience. The lineage graph starts from the source folder node, which feeds your bronze view and everything downstream: Select the source folder node to see the OneLake path and the files discovered in it. Select the file-ingesting view to inspect its format, schema mode, and refresh mode. Drill into any run to see how many files were processed and rows added — so you can confirm new data was picked up. Pair that with the __filepath__ column to reconcile row counts back to individual source files: SELECT __filepath__, COUNT(*) AS rows FROM bronze.raw_orders GROUP BY __filepath__; Schema on your terms File-ingesting materialized lake views support two schema modes, allowing you to choose between automatic schema evolution and a fixed schema contract: `DYNAMIC` (default): the view schema evolves with your data — new columns are added and dropped columns handled automatically across files and refreshes. Perfect for landing zones where source shape changes over time. `FIXED` : the schema is pinned at creation and drift is rejected — ideal when you need a stable contract for downstream consumers. Refresh and scheduling, handled for you Just like table-based materialized lake views, you don't orchestrate file ingestion from a notebook. Use lineage and scheduled refresh on the lakehouse to run views in dependency order and pick up new files automatically. Need to reprocess an entire folder on demand? A single full refresh does it: REFRESH MATERIALIZED LAKE VIEW bronze.raw_orders FULL; Key benefits Together, these capabilities help simplify file-based ingestion and bring raw files into the same declarative workflow as the rest of your medallion architecture. One declarative model — from raw files to gold, no separate ingestion step to build or operate. Bronze in a single statement — replace bespoke COPY/pipeline/notebook loaders with USING OneLake_Files. End-to-end lineage — trace data from the source folder, through every layer, down to the individual file. Built-in data quality and scheduling — the same governance and orchestration you already rely on for table-based views. Schema flexibility — evolve automatically with DYNAMIC or lock a contract with FIXED. Get started Open a lakehouse in Microsoft Fabric and drop your CSV or Parquet files into Files . Create a file-ingesting materialized lake view with USING OneLake_Files. Build silver and gold views on top, then schedule a refresh from the Materialized lake views → Manage experience. Resources What are materialized lake views in Microsoft Fabric? Spark SQL reference for materialized lake views Manage materialized lake views lineage Tutorial: Build a medallion architecture with materialized lake views Tell us what you think We built file data ingestion to make the first mile of your medallion pipeline as effortless as the rest of it. Try it out on your own CSV and Parquet data and share your feedback on the Fabric Community — we can't wait to see the pipelines you build.

title: Fabric App functions to use secure server-side custom logic (Preview)
text: Fabric App functions  is a new capability that allows builders to add secure, server-side logic directly to their Fabric Apps without standing up separate infrastructure. Built on top of Fabric User Data Functions (UDFs), Fabric App functions give developers a simple way to execute business logic, integrate with external services, access protected resources, and keep secrets from the client. Figure: Get started with functions in your Fabric app. What are Fabric App functions? Fabric App functions are TypeScript-based serverless functions that run alongside your Fabric app. They provide a secure backend execution environment for code that should not run in the browser. Functions are packaged and deployed as part of the application experience and can be invoked directly from the application through a typed client. Think of Functions as the custom logic layer for your Fabric App: Execute business rules and complex calculations Access protected data sources Call external APIs Perform orchestration and AI workflows Store and retrieve secrets securely Access downstream resources using the application’s identity via application authentication Application authentication Application authentication means the Fabric app function accesses a downstream resource using the application’s identity rather than impersonating the person currently using the app. The downstream service sees and authorizes the application, not the signed-in user. How the identity flow works The user signs in to the Fabric App, the app calls the function, and the function then calls the downstream service using the application identity. Grant the application only the permissions it needs. Authorize the application at the downstream service. Keep credentials and tokens out of client-side code. Add application-level validation and business logic before accessing data. Secrets management Functions allow builders to securely store and retrieve secrets without exposing them to browsers or application users. Figure: Add and manage secrets for Fabric app functions. Get started with functions Fabric App functions are designed to feel like part of the application, not a separate platform. Key dependency is to install Azure Functions Core Tools version 4 before you get started. npm install --global azure-functions-core-tools@4 Create an app with functions Scaffold a new app, move to the app directory, and initialize its functions project: npm create @microsoft/rayfin@latest -- "my-app" cd my-app npx rayfin functions init The Fabric App functions init command adds the functions project, TypeScript configuration, and a starter function file to the existing app. Build the app with GitHub Copilot The scaffold includes the GitHub Copilot instructions and skills needed to work with the project. Open the project in Visual Studio Code, then describe the app you want to build in GitHub Copilot Chat. For example, use this prompt to build an AI pull request review assistant: Build an app that lets me view all pull requests for the repository <repoURL>, chat with my Azure AI Foundry agent <agentName> to review pull requests, and post review comments. Use functions with application authentication to connect to Azure AI Foundry and Azure DevOps. GitHub Copilot can generate and update the required files and components. You can also ask the agent to run the app, debug functions locally, and deploy the app. Debug functions You can run functions locally to test your server-side logic before deploying to Fabric. Use the local Azure functions host to invoke functions, inspect errors, and validate your integration. Once validated, deploy the app and functions together. Run the following command to test your functions and deploy your changes. npx rayfin dev npx rayfin up Conclusion If you’ve been waiting for a secure way to connect Fabric Apps to external services, protect secrets, use application authentication, or build AI-powered experiences, Fabric App functions are the missing piece. To learn more, refer to the Fabric Apps documentation.

title: My workspace governance improvements (Generally Available)
text: My workspace governance features , which give administrators governance controls over their users' personal My workspaces, are now generally available.   As My workspaces continue to be used for business-critical content, organizations need governance capabilities that scale with their environment. These enhancements give administrators greater flexibility to access, manage, and recover content when needed, while enabling automation that reduces operational overhead and improves consistency across the tenant. These enhanced tenant administrator controls for My workspace are also available in government clouds.  What's new  Two new admin REST APIs make temporary admin access to a personal workspace fully programmable:  Grant Admin Temporary Access : grants a Fabric administrator 24-hour access to a user's My workspace. Remove Admin Temporary Access :  revokes that access before the 24-hour window ends.  Both can be called by a Fabric administrator or by a service principal. The service principal identity must be enabled for Admin API access in your tenant settings. SPN support and these new APIs allow tenant administrators to automate management of tenant users’ My workspaces contents instead of doing it by hand in the Admin Portal.  Reminder: Restoring orphaned My workspaces  When a user is hard deleted in Microsoft Entra, their My workspace becomes orphaned and moves to a Deleted state, with contents retained for 30 days . During that window, you can restore it with the Restore Workspace API.   Important: new workspace name is required when restoring a former My workspace, and you assign a new admin to own the recovered content.  Try the Admin controls and new APIs and let us know what you think in the comment section.

title: What’s new for Business Events and real-time events in Microsoft Fabric
text: Microsoft Fabric helps teams react when those moments happen. Real-Time Hub provides a common place to discover event sources, connect consumers, and move from a signal to an action. With Business Events now generally available and new Fabric Events capabilities arriving in the September 2026 release, organizations can connect business meaning and platform operations through one event-driven model. One model, three outcomes Publish a governed signal once, let operational teams react independently, and retain the same event for real-time and historical analysis. Turn business meaning into a governed event (Generally Available) A Business Event represents a meaningful occurrence or state change that matters to the organization. It is not raw telemetry or a diagnostic record. It captures business intent: a payment failed, a cold-chain shipment is at risk, inventory fell below a threshold, or an approval is required. Every Business Event follows a versioned schema in an Event Schema Set. Publishers and consumers agree on the event name, fields, data types, and meaning before they integrate. This contract reduces point-to-point dependencies because the publisher does not need to know which teams will react, and consumer teams can add or change their responses without modifying publisher code. Use the Fabric experience closest to the business logic Business Events meet teams where their detection logic already runs. A notebook can publish the result of analytics or machine learning. A User Data Function can emit an event from reusable domain logic after validating an application request. Activator can convert a condition detected in Power BI, a Real-Time Dashboard, KQL, or a warehouse query into a governed signal. This flexibility keeps ownership clear. The team that understands the business condition owns when the event is published. The Event Schema Set owns the shared contract. Downstream teams own how they respond. The following animation follows a cold-chain shipment risk event through Real-Time Hub. It shows how a user opens the governed event, reviews its schema and connected consumers, publishes representative data, and verifies the event flow before relying on production logic. Figure: The Business Events experience in Real-Time Hub brings the event contract, publishers, consumers, and validation tools into one workflow. By bringing the event contract, publishers, consumers, and validation tools into one experience, Real-Time Hub gives teams a shared view of how an event moves through the system. Teams can use that visibility to confirm that the event structure and connections work as expected before the production publisher is ready. Validate integrations before production code is ready A faster inner loop is one of the most practical advantages of the new experience. The sample publisher generates a JSON payload from the selected schema, so teams can replace the values or upload a representative file and publish an event in seconds. Data preview then shows recent payloads for each publisher and consumer together with event metadata and the active schema version. Teams can publish a sample Business Event , inspect Business Events data , and verify the contract, permissions, subscription, and routing before connecting the live publisher. This removes temporary test code and gives both sides of the integration direct evidence that the expected payload arrived. For application-oriented scenarios, the guided User Data Function publisher experience prepares the Fabric connection and sample publisher code from Real-Time Hub. Developers can focus on the business condition and payload instead of integration plumbing. Process, act, and analyze without changing the publisher After an event is published, independent consumers can choose the response that matches their responsibility. Activator can send notifications, start workflows, or invoke downstream logic. Eventhouse can retain every event in a dedicated Kusto Query Language (KQL) table for operational monitoring, historical analysis, Real-Time Dashboards, anomaly detection, and AI or machine learning scenarios. React immediately to a high-severity condition with an alert or automated action. Route and transform the signal for downstream destinations through Eventstream. Retain durable evidence for audit, trends, service-level analysis, and continuous improvement. Eventstream as a Business Events consumer is in Preview. It can filter, enrich, transform, route, and fan out an existing governed signal while the original publisher remains independent. Teams can add Business Events from an Eventstream or start from the event in Real-Time Hub through a prepopulated consumer flow. Review the Eventstream consumer guidance for configuration details. For the generally available paths, learn how to publish Business Events from Activator and analyze Business Events in Eventhouse . Monitor capacity health as events occur (Generally Available) Capacity Overview Events include two event types. Capacity Summary events provide a recurring high-level view of utilization and health, while Capacity State events identify changes such as pause, resume, and throttling-related conditions. Capacity administrators no longer need to rely only on periodic checks to discover that action may be required. These signals can drive no-code alerts in Activator, automated workflows, or Eventstream processing. They can also land in Eventhouse for KQL analysis, historical retention, and dashboards that help teams recognize patterns before users are affected. Figure: Capacity Overview Events expose capacity state and summary signals that administrators can connect to alerts, processing, and analysis. Follow the capacity health monitoring tutorial and review the Capacity Overview Events schema to get started. Find the operations driving capacity pressure (Preview) Capacity Operation Events extend capacity visibility from overall health to operation-level root cause. Fabric emits an event for each operation that consumes capacity, with details such as the workspace and item, capacity unit consumption, duration, throttling delay, status, and smoothing-window attribution. Administrators can identify which refreshes consumed the most capacity, which operations were throttled, and where repeated failures originate. Activator can respond when an expensive operation crosses a threshold, while Eventstream and Eventhouse support routing, chargeback analysis, governance, and longer-term optimization. Figure: Capacity Operation Events add operation-level context for troubleshooting utilization, throttling, and failures. Review the Capacity Operation Events documentation for the complete schema. React to item deletion and recovery (Generally Available) Real-Time Hub now includes workspace item lifecycle events for soft-delete and recovery operations. Teams can subscribe when an item is moved into the recovery state, when recovery succeeds, or when either operation fails. These events make item lifecycle activity available to the same alerting and stream-processing tools already used for other Fabric Events. A workspace administrator can receive an alert when a critical item is accidentally soft deleted, trigger a governance workflow, or retain the event for audit and historical analysis. Because the new events use the existing workspace item event model, teams can extend current consumers instead of building a separate monitoring path. Figure: Workspace item events now include soft-delete and recovery outcomes for real-time notification, automation, and governance. Explore the Fabric workspace item events documentation for event names and schema details. title: A new look and new capabilities in the Capacity Metrics App (Preview)
text: As announced at FabCon 2026 in Barcelona, we're releasing meaningful enhancements to the Capacity Metrics app in preview, designed to accelerate time to insight. This includes new and enhanced visuals and metrics across the health, compute, and storage pages—alongside improved navigation and a refreshed user interface design. A new item details page builds on the existing item history page, providing key insights for individual items running on the capacity. The aim is to support key user journeys, including: Identifying issues as they happen. Reviewing issues that have occurred over the last two weeks. Identifying risks before they result in throttling. Improved experiences An admin can now land on the health page and quickly identify capacities most in need of review. New metrics introduce easily understandable concepts like percentage of time spent in throttling, which can be compared across capacities and time periods. Figure: Health summary page displaying capacity health statistics for various services like Health, Compute, Storage, and Autoscale for Spark, with columns for different time periods, utilization, and various types of throttling – providing the capacity admin a view across capacities to help them keep operations smooth. Once a capacity is identified for further review, the new compute page provides rich detail on the health state of the capacity and the biggest items impacting the capacity for the selected period. Key new visuals include: An updated utilization graph which expresses capacity unit (CU) consumption in CU seconds rather than a percentage, making it easy to see if your capacity has been scaled up or down, while also showing the current throttling state through conditional formatting. A new heat map visual that shows the capacities most utilized/overutilized state for each hour, making it easy to spot daily or hourly patterns. A new CU consumption table, which shows the item impacting the time window being reviewed (to a granularity of 1 hour). The visual shows smoothed CU consumption, meaning this truly reflects the highest impact items for the time being reviewed. Figure: Compute dashboard with various metrics related to Fabric Capacity, including smoothed and unsmoothed usage percentages, time paused, and time no throttling, as well as different types of rejections and surge protection, all within a specified date range. Once an item is identified as a possible cause of high utilization, or if the user just wants to see additional detail on the item, the new item details page provides a 14-day history. The page has been designed from the ground up to give detailed insights which were previously unavailable. One key visual is the new CU utilization chart which shows the impact the selected item had on the overall capacity. Figure: Item details page including a column chart shows the impact the selected item is having on the capacity as a whole, aggregated CU usage across different fields such as users, and detailed information on consumption for the selected item. Given the new experiences include changes to the existing metrics, it is being released as a preview alongside the existing app generally available experience, allowing time for you to adapt to the new app while still having access to the existing version. When you install the new version of the app, you will see the new preview as an additional option alongside the existing generally available versions of the reports. Select  Get it from the notification to update your current installation or install the latest version in a new workspace. Alternatively, you can install the app directly from the Microsoft Marketplace . We're excited to put these new capabilities into your hands and look forward to your feedback as we continue evolving the Capacity Metrics experience to help you better understand, manage, and optimize your Fabric capacities.

title: Custom SQL Pools in Fabric Data Warehouse (Generally Available)
text: Custom SQL Pools in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse are now generally available, along with statement type classification. Custom SQL Pools give administrators more control over how compute resources are allocated across different workloads in a Fabric workspace. You can isolate workloads into separate pools, set maximum resource allocation percentages, and help ensure that one workload doesn’t consume resources intended for another. For example, you can create separate pools for data ingestion, reporting, and ad hoc analysis, then configure the maximum percentage of compute resources each pool can consume. Custom SQL Pools complement the autonomous workload-management capabilities built into Fabric Data Warehouse while giving organizations additional control for predictable and business-critical workloads. Classify workloads by statement type Statement type classification provides a simple way to separate read and write workloads. When configuring Custom SQL Pools, you can classify distributed SQL requests into two categories: SELECT for read queries. NONSELECT for statements such as data loading and modification operations. Fabric creates separate pools for the two statement categories, with an initial maximum allocation of 50% for each pool. Administrators can adjust these percentages based on workload requirements, provided their combined maximum allocation doesn’t exceed 100%. Statement type classification is useful when organizations want to protect interactive reporting capacity from intensive ingestion or data-transformation workloads without relying on application names or connection properties. Custom SQL Pools also support application-based classification using an exact application name or a regular expression. Administrators can select the classification model that best reflects how workloads connect to and use their Fabric workspace. Get started To learn about Custom SQL Pools, supported classifiers, resource allocation, and workload behavior, review the Custom SQL Pools documentation. For instructions to create and configure pools in the Fabric portal, review the Configure Custom SQL Pools in the Fabric Portal documentation.
